open_questions: Going to a Go-Go, Shop Around and Mickey's Monkey have no human drum part on Songsterr (Going to a Go-Go no drum track at all), and a fold of Going to a Go-Go's record did not settle where its bar begins. You Can't Hurry Love is reconstructed from the record and a machine tab: a human transcription would settle its kick and its pickups.
Who played on which Motown record: Motown credited no musicians until 1971; the credits here are Wikipedia's (Allan Slutsky's Standing in the Shadows of Motown is the usual source, not read).
Uptight: Wikipedia's song article credits him, his own notes that some sources credit Pistol Allen.
His birth date: 25 July 1925 (Wikipedia, Drummerszone) or 15 July.
His brushwork: Loudlands says he often used brushes on records; no record of his with brushes was identified.
His kit: no photograph of his drums was found; the studio set was second-hand and of mixed makes.

identity.name: Benny Benjamin

evidence.note: Wikipedia gives 25 July and notes sources giving 15 July.

identity.summary: Motown's first studio drummer, from 1958, and the Funk Brothers' drummer on its early hits: Money, Do You Love Me, My Girl, I Can't Help Myself, Uptight, Going to a Go-Go, Get Ready, You Can't Hurry Love. A big-band drummer by training, influenced by Buddy Rich and Tito Puente, he played plain, steady time with James Jamerson ('he kept the tempo better than a metronome', Berry Gordy) and started the Motown pickup, the burst on the snare into the next phrase. Producers would not cut a session without him and Jamerson. Drink and heroin cost him the chair to Uriel Jones and Pistol Allen; he died in 1969, at 43. Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, 2003.

traditions.impact: He learned the drums in the style of the big bands, after Buddy Rich and Tito Puente; at Motown he told Pistol Allen to 'leave the jazz drumming at home'.

formative_events.event: Motown's first studio drummer, with Berry Gordy from the start.
Money (That's What I Want), Motown's first hit, from a jam in Studio A.
Motown buys a permanent second-hand kit for Studio A; he once pawned it, convincing the night watchman it was his.
His last run of hits (Get Ready, You Can't Hurry Love) as Uriel Jones and Pistol Allen take more of the dates.

eras.label: Motown's Studio A
eras.context: Hitsville U.S.A., Detroit: the Funk Brothers with James Jamerson on bass, Jack Ashford or Brian Holland on tambourine, cutting the label's singles for Gordy, Smokey Robinson and Holland–Dozier–Holland.
defining_traits: the snare on every beat for a dance record
the pickup on the snare into the phrase

evidence.note: Gordy: 'He had a pulse, a steadiness, that kept the tempo better than a metronome.'

swing.notes: Straight eighths on every record read; the shuffles at Motown were Pistol Allen's, by the forum accounts (not used).

dynamics.balance: Under the singer: 'he makes it breathe' (Modern Drummer, 2009); 'control of dynamics' (Loudlands).

feel_profile.interaction: With James Jamerson: the pickups were made to fit between his drums and Jamerson's bass (Uriel Jones).

hand_techniques.name: The Motown pickup
hand_techniques.description: A burst of sixteenths on the snare (and the toms) on the last beat or two of a phrase, into the next: I Can't Help Myself's four on 4, Uptight's on 3 and 4, Get Ready's from the 'and' of 3 into every second bar of the chorus.

hand_techniques.name: The snare on every beat
hand_techniques.description: For a dance record, the snare on all four beats: under the hat on the 'and's (Uptight), under eighths in the choruses of Get Ready and Nowhere to Run, and all through You Can't Hurry Love.

hand_techniques.name: Eighths on the hat or the ride
hand_techniques.description: Under a backbeat on 2 and 4 (My Girl, Do You Love Me, Money).

hand_techniques.name: Brushes
hand_techniques.description: Often on records, by one account; none identified here.

foot_techniques.name: The kick under the bass
foot_techniques.description: On 1 and 3 with an 'and' or two where Jamerson's line has them (My Girl's 'and' of 3, Do You Love Me's 'and' of 4). Nowhere to Run's kick on the 'and's of 2 and 4.

devices_search.note: None found. His playing is a steady backbeat, the snare on every beat for a dance record, and the pickup into the phrase: feel and fills, not a device. Do You Love Me's stops and Money's floor tom are arrangement.

voice_language.snare: The backbeat on 2 and 4, or on every beat (Uptight); a sixteenth burst into the next phrase.
voice_language.kick: On 1 and 3 with the bass line's 'and's.
voice_language.toms: The high and mid toms finishing a pickup (Uptight, My Girl); Money's high tom on 4 and floor tom at the turn.
voice_language.hihat: Eighths, opened on an 'and' (Do You Love Me); on the 'and's under the snare (Uptight).
voice_language.cymbals: The ride in eighths for a chorus or a whole record (Money); a crash on the first bar of a section.

aesthetic: a second-hand kit of mixed makes
the tambourine on the backbeat beside the snare

by_era.description: Hitsville's Studio A, the 'snake pit': a studio set of Ludwig, Slingerland, Rogers and Gretsch parts.

sample_hints.60s: A 1960s American kit, round and warm, close and a little roomy.

signature_traits.label: The Motown pickup
signature_traits.description: The sixteenths on the snare into the next phrase, 'sampled more than any drum pickups ever'; Uriel Jones says Benjamin originated them.

signature_traits.label: Better than a metronome
signature_traits.description: Berry Gordy: 'He had a pulse, a steadiness, that kept the tempo better than a metronome.'

signature_traits.label: The snare on every beat
signature_traits.description: Uptight's snare on all four beats under the hat on the 'and's.

signature_traits.label: Simple time that breathes
signature_traits.description: 'You don't have to be wild to play'; plain time that leaves the singer room and makes the odd lick stand out.

patterns.name: Money: the snare on 2, the tom on 4
patterns.function: The ride in eighths, the snare on 2 alone, the high tom on 4 and its 'and' with the kick, the kick on 1 and 3: the tambourine has the 4.

patterns.name: Money: the floor tom at the turn
patterns.function: The floor tom in eighths, the kick on 1 and 3, for four bars at the riff's turn.

patterns.name: Do You Love Me: the dance
patterns.function: Eighths on the hat, opened on the 'and' of 3, the snare on 2, its 'and' and 4, the kick on 1, 3, its 'and' and the 'and' of 4.

patterns.name: Do You Love Me: the band's stop
patterns.function: The snare and the floor tom together on 1 and 4, the kick on 1, under 'do you love me?'.

evidence.note: The tab writes the hat with them too; three hands, so the hat is left out.

patterns.name: My Girl: the verse
patterns.function: Eighths on the hat, the snare on 2 and 4, the kick on 1, 3 and its 'and'.

evidence.note: 21 of the tab's 62 bars; the 2026 tab agrees.

patterns.name: My Girl: the pickup after the bass
patterns.function: Three sixteenths on the snare from the 'and' of 3, the mid tom and the kick on the 'and' of 4.

evidence.note: Off the grid in the tab (a sixteenth triplet's three); here three sixteenths.

patterns.name: Uptight: the snare on every beat
patterns.function: The snare on every beat, the hat on the 'and's, the kick on 1 and the 'and's of 2, 3 and 4.

evidence.note: The chorus and the verses, most of the tab's 97 bars.

patterns.name: Uptight: the pickup into the next bar
patterns.function: The snare on 1 and 2, four sixteenths on 3, four on the high tom on 4.

patterns.name: I Can't Help Myself: the kick on 1 and 3
patterns.function: The kick on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4 with the hat on 2 and the foot on 4.

patterns.name: The Motown pickup
patterns.function: Four sixteenths on the snare on 4 at the end of an eight-bar phrase, into the next: the fill Uriel Jones credits to him.

evidence.note: I Can't Help Myself, bars 6, 14, 22 and on; Uriel Jones names the pickups as Benjamin's.

patterns.name: Get Ready: the chorus pickup
patterns.function: The snare on 1, 2 and 3, three sixteenths from the 'and' of 3, the kick on the 'and' of 4: every second bar of the chorus.

patterns.name: Nowhere to Run
patterns.function: Eighths on the hat, the backbeat, the kick on 1, the 'and' of 2, 3 and the 'and' of 4.

patterns.name: You Can't Hurry Love
patterns.function: The snare on every beat, eighths on the hat, the kick on 1 and the 'and's of 2, 3 and 4.

evidence.note: Reconstructed: the record folded onto a sixteenth grid ten seconds at a time (the snare level on every beat, the hat on beats and 'and's only, the kick strongest on the 'and's of 2, 3 and 4), agreeing with the snare of a machine tab moved by one of its beats. No human transcription.

equipment.label: Studio A's kit, 1960s
equipment.layout_notes: A second-hand studio set of Ludwig, Slingerland, Rogers and Gretsch parts; before 1963 he brought his own kit down the studio steps. Sizes and finishes not found.

affiliations.name: The Funk Brothers
affiliations.notes: Motown's studio band at Hitsville U.S.A., uncredited on the records until 1971.

evidence.note: Jones modelled his playing on Benjamin's and was used on most tunes after him for having cloned his approach.
Told him to 'leave the jazz drumming at home, hold down simple beats'.
'I learned from just listening to him.'
Gordy and Jamerson would not work a session without him.

philosophy.idea: Leave the jazz at home: hold down simple beats.
Keep the focus on the singer; simple time makes the odd lick stand out.

innovations: The Motown pickup into the phrase, by Uriel Jones's account
The Motown studio beat under the label's first hits, with James Jamerson

cultural_references.description: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, 2003 (sidemen).
Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002), in archive stills.
Rolling Stone's eleventh greatest drummer of all time, 2016.

common_misconceptions: That every Motown drum track is his: from the mid-1960s Uriel Jones and Pistol Allen played many of them (Baby Love is Allen's).

beatbreaker.default_kit_sound: A 1960s American kit in a small room
generation_rules: A plain backbeat, or the snare on every beat for a dance record.
Eighths on the hat or the ride; the kick with the bass line.
A pickup of sixteenths on the snare into the next phrase; few other fills.

lineage_display.lineage_blurb: Big-band swing after Buddy Rich and Tito Puente, simplified into the Motown studio beat, which Uriel Jones and Pistol Allen carried on after him.
